title: Storage Class
body:
The keyword on a declaration that picks a [[Variable]]'s [[Variable Lifetime|lifetime]] and
how far its name reaches.

| Keyword | Lifetime | Visibility |
|---|---|---|
| *(none, local)* | automatic: the enclosing block | that block |
| `static` on a local | whole program | still just that block |
| `static` on a global | whole program | this file only |
| *(none, global)* | whole program | every file, with `extern` |
| `extern` | whole program | declares one defined elsewhere |

Two uses of `static`, which is the confusing part: on a local it *extends* the lifetime, on a
global it *restricts* the visibility. Same word, opposite jobs.

```c++
int count_calls() {
	static int n = 0;   // initialised once, survives every return
	return ++n;
}
```

Storage class is the mechanism; [[Variable Scope]] and [[Variable Lifetime]] are the two
questions it answers, and they are worth reading first. Nothing here touches the heap:
`new` and `delete` are not storage classes, they are [[Dynamic Allocation]] and the lifetime
is whatever you make it.

`const` is not a storage class either, it is a promise not to assign. It travels with the
declaration and is worth using on every array size and every reference parameter you do not
intend to write through.
